sections.title: The Dead in Sin and Made Alive in Christ
observations: Paul begins by reminding the Ephesians of their former state before coming to faith in Christ. They were spiritually dead, living in sin and following the ways of the world and the devil. This emphasizes the total depravity of humanity and the need for divine intervention.
The phrase 'made alive' signifies the transformative power of God’s grace. It is not by their own works that they are saved, but through faith in Christ, who has raised them from spiritual death.

sections.title: Saved by Grace Through Faith
observations: This section highlights the core doctrine of salvation by grace through faith. Paul stresses that salvation is a gift from God, not a result of human effort or merit. This is foundational to the Reformed understanding of soteriology.
The purpose of salvation is not only personal but also to create a new community of believers, the Church, which is to reflect God’s glory.

sections.title: Unity in Christ
observations: Paul discusses the breaking down of the dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles. In Christ, all believers are united, regardless of their ethnic or cultural backgrounds. This unity is a central theme in Ephesians and reflects the inclusive nature of the Gospel.
The Church is described as a holy temple, built together for God’s dwelling. This imagery emphasizes the communal aspect of salvation and the importance of the Church in God’s redemptive plan.

importantVerses.commentary: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, highlights the character of God as merciful and loving, which is the foundation of our salvation.
For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, emphasizes the doctrine of salvation by grace alone, a key tenet of Reformed theology.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, underscores the new identity and community believers have in Christ.

questions: What does it mean to be 'dead in sin' and how does this affect our understanding of human nature?
How does the concept of grace challenge our views on merit and works in relation to salvation?
In what ways can the Church today reflect the unity that Paul describes between Jews and Gentiles?
